passage.title: Exploring Space
passage.content:
Space is a vast and mysterious place filled with wonders. Scientists have studied _____(1)_____ for many years to understand how the planets, stars, and other objects move and interact. Our planet Earth is just one of many _____(2)_____ that travel around the Sun.

At night, we can see many bright stars in the sky. These _____(3)_____ are huge balls of burning gas, and they are much farther away than the moon. The _____(4)_____ is Earth's closest neighbor in space, and it reflects the light of the Sun.

To study the moon, stars, and faraway planets, scientists use a tool called a telescope. A _____(5)_____ helps people see things that are very far away. It collects light and brings the image closer so we can learn more about objects in space. They enjoy learning about the movements of planets and how _____(6)_____ travels across space to reach our eyes.

Our office is looking for someone organized and reliable to help with admin tasks. You'll answer phones, support different projects, and keep things running smoothly. You need to know Microsoft Office and have strong communication skills. This is a full-time role with benefits.

We're looking for someone caring and enthusiastic to support teaching children in a fun setting. Experience with kids is a plus but not required. It's a part-time job with flexible hours—and a chance to really make a difference in children's lives.

parts.title: PART 3

paragraphs.content: Today Jakarta has much to offer, ranging from museums, art and antique markets, first class shopping to accommodations and a wide variety of cultural activities. Jakarta's most famous landmark, the National Monument or Monas is a 137m obelisk topped with a flame sculpture coated with 35 kg of gold. Among other places one can mention the National museum that holds an extensive collection of ethnographic artifacts and relics, the Maritime Museum that exhibits Indonesia's seafaring traditions, including models of sea going vessels.

Sumatra is a paradise for nature lovers, its national parks are the largest in the world, home to a variety of monkeys, tigers and elephants. Facing the open sea, the western coastline of Sumatra and the waters surrounding Nias Island have big waves that make them one of the best surfer's beaches in Indonesia. There are beautiful coral reefs that are ideal for diving. For those who prefer night dives, the waters of Riau Archipelago offer a rewarding experience with marine scavengers of the dark waters.

Various establishments offer professional pampering service with floral baths, body scrubs, aromatic oils, massages and meditation; rituals and treatments that use spices and aromatic herbs to promote physical and mental wellness. Various spa hotels are extremely popular. Indonesians believe that when treating the body you cure the mind.

Jakarta has a distinctly cosmopolitan flavor. Tantalize your taste buds with a gastronomic spree around the city's many eateries. Like French gourmet dining, exotic Asian cuisine, American fast food, stylish cafes, restaurants all compete to find a way into your heart through your stomach. The taste of Indonesia's many cultures can be found in almost any corner of the city: hot and spicy food from West Sumatra, sweet tastes of Dental Java, the tangy fish dishes of North Sulawesi.

In the face of constant exposure to modernization and foreign influences, the native people still faithfully cling to their culture and rituals. The pre-Hindu Bali Aga tribe still maintains their own traditions of architecture, pagan religion, dance and music, such as unique rituals of dances and gladiator-like battles between youths. On the island of Siberut native tribes have retained their Neolithic hunter-gathering culture.

Whether you are a serious spender or half hearted shopper, there is sure to be something for everybody in Jakarta. Catering to diverse tastes and pockets, the wide variety of things you can buy in Jakarta is mind boggling from the best of local handicrafts to haute couture labels. Modern super and hyper markets, multi-level shopping centers, retail and specialty shops, sell quality goods at a competitive price. Sidewalk bargains range from tropical blooms of vivid colors and scents in attractive bouquets to luscious fruits of the seasons.

passage.title: The world's rich nations miss a golden opportunity
passage.content:
In a speech in October 2001, the British Prime Minister, Tony Blair, suggested that there would be a radical change of policy on Africa. "The current state of Africa", he said, "is a scar on the conscience of the world. But if the whole world focused on it, we could heal that scar. And if we don't focus on it, it will become deeper and angrier."

So I would like to ask Britain's prime minister to explain his actions at the G8 summit in France last week. A few weeks ago President Jacques Chirac did something amazing. After years of opposing any changes to European farm subsidies, he approached the US government to suggest that Europe would stop subsidising its exports of food to Africa if America did the same. This was an important offer, not only because it represented a significant change of policy for France, but also because it provided an opportunity for both the European Union and the US to abandon their constant attempts to offer higher agricultural subsidies than each other. As Blair has pointed out, the West's agricultural subsidies are a disaster for the developing world, and particularly for Africa. Farming accounts for some 70% of employment in Africa, and most of the farmers there are extremely poor. Part of the reason for this is that the prices of products grown by African farmers are unfairly undercut by the subsidised products dumped on their markets by exporters from the US and the EU.

So we might have expected Blair to have welcomed Chirac's initiative. Instead the prime minister single-handedly destroyed it. The reason is, of course, familiar. George Bush receives a great deal of political support from US agro-industrialists, grain exporters and pesticide manufacturers, and he was not prepared to match Chirac's offer. If the EU, and in particular the UK, had supported France, it would have been difficult for Bush to oppose the idea. But as soon as Blair made it clear that he would not support Chirac's plan, the initiative was dead.

So, thanks to Mr Blair and his habit of doing whatever Bush tells him to, Africa will continue to suffer. The basic problem is that the rich nations fix the global trade rules. The current world trade agreement was supposed to have prevented the EU and the US from subsidising their exports to developing nations. But the agreement contains so many loopholes that it permits the US and the EU simply to call their export subsidies by a different name.

The EU has stopped paying farmers for what they produce and started instead to give them direct grants, based on the amount of land they own and how much they produced there in the past. The US does the same and has also introduced some new tricks. One of these is called "export credit": the state reduces the cost of US exports by providing cheap insurance for the exporters. These credits are worth some $7.7bn to US grain sellers. This money ensures that American exporters can undercut the world price for wheat and maize by between 10% and 16%, and the world price for cotton by 40%.

But the worst of its hidden export subsidies is its use of international aid as a means of entering the markets of poorer nations. Other countries give money and the World Food Programme can use this money to buy supplies in local markets, which helps local farmers at the same time as feeding starving people. The US, on the other hand, sends its own subsidised food instead of money, saying that this programme will "develop and expand commercial markets for US products".

passage.title: Volcanoes
passage.content:
Volcanoes are among the most powerful and dramatic natural forces on Earth. They form when molten rock, ash, and gases escape from deep within the planet's crust through weak points or fractures. This molten material, known as magma, becomes lava once it erupts onto the surface. Volcanic activity has shaped the Earth's surface for millions of years, creating entire continents, islands, and mountain ranges. While often viewed as destructive, volcanoes are in fact fundamental to the planet's long-term geological and ecological evolution. The minerals released during eruptions contribute to soil formation, and the gases they emit play a role in regulating Earth's atmosphere. In this way, volcanoes are both builders and destroyers, highlighting the delicate balance between creation and collapse in the natural world.

Historically, volcanic eruptions have had profound consequences. The eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD buried the Roman cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum, preserving them in volcanic ash for future discovery. Krakatoa's 1883 explosion generated massive tsunamis and altered global weather patterns for years. More recently, the 2010 eruption of Iceland's Eyjafjallajökull disrupted international air travel, reminding the modern world that nature's forces remain far beyond our control. Volcanoes typically form along tectonic plate boundaries, where plates collide, pull apart, or slide past one another. The intense pressure and heat in these zones melt the mantle, forming magma. When this magma finds a path to the surface, it results in an eruption. These eruptions can be gentle or violent, depending on the magma's composition, temperature, gas content, and viscosity.

There are several types of volcanoes, each with distinct features and eruption styles. Shield volcanoes, such as Mauna Loa in Hawaii, have wide bases and produce slow, fluid lava flows. Stratovolcanoes, including Mount Fuji and Mount Etna, are steep-sided and capable of highly explosive eruptions. Cinder cones are small, simple structures formed from ash and debris. Calderas, on the other hand, are large depressions formed after the collapse of a magma chamber following a massive eruption.

Despite their destructive potential, volcanoes offer numerous benefits. Volcanic ash is rich in minerals and contributes to the formation of extremely fertile soil, supporting agriculture in countries like Indonesia and Italy. Additionally, volcanic regions are often rich in geothermal energy, providing a sustainable source of electricity and heating. Volcanic rocks are used in construction, and unique volcanic landscapes fuel tourism, bringing economic advantages to local communities.

However, the hazards associated with volcanic eruptions are significant and should not be underestimated. Lava flows can destroy infrastructure and natural ecosystems. Ash clouds can collapse buildings, contaminate water supplies, and disrupt aviation. Toxic gases like sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide pose serious health risks. Pyroclastic flows—fast-moving currents of hot gas and volcanic matter—are among the deadliest consequences of an eruption.

Modern science has made considerable progress in monitoring and forecasting volcanic activity. Seismographs detect ground vibrations caused by rising magma. Gas sensors analyze changes in volcanic emissions. Satellite imagery and thermal cameras help observe ground deformation and temperature increases. For example, a sudden increase in sulfur dioxide may indicate that magma is nearing the surface. Earthquakes often precede eruptions, and ground swelling can signal pressure building within the volcano.
